content: The diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) characteristics of Ov-16 serology are more reliable than those of skin snip microscopy, particularly in regions with low onchocerciasis prevalence due to mass drug administration (MDA). The results of 36 diagnostic studies using skin snip microscopy as the gold-standard reference test are considered unreliable due to a high risk of bias. Additionally, DTA values for skin snip microscopy, when used as an index test against Ov-16 serology as the reference test, are provided in Appendix C. The DTA values of Ov-16 serology are influenced by the prevalence of onchocerciasis and vary across age groups, as the test does not differentiate between past and active infections. Ov-16 serology measures exposure to Onchocerca volvulus and indirectly detects transmission, which introduces a degree of evidence indirectness. Graphical representations of the sensitivity and specificity of Ov-16 serology compared to skin snip microscopy are shown in Figure 4. The upper left corner of the graph represents optimal DTA values (high sensitivity and specificity), while the lower right corner represents poor DTA values (low sensitivity and specificity). Detailed results of the risk of bias and applicability assessments, as well as other GRADE domains, are presented in Table 6 and GRADE profile 3. The DTA values of Ov-16 serology (index test) versus O-150 PCR (index test) are also compared. Black flies were collected from various regions in Africa and Mexico (Chiapas), and different species of Simulium black flies were analyzed. These flies originated from endemic regions, but there was variability in vector control measures, timing of collection, and infectivity rates. No statistically significant differences in diagnostic accuracy were observed between O-150 PCR (PoolScreen) and dissection of flies. Similarly, no differences were found between newer DNA extraction methods with larger pool sizes and traditional methods. The included studies did not allow for the calculation of sensitivity and specificity. The overall quality of evidence from diagnostic studies for this comparison is moderate, as shown in GRADE profile 4. Studies were conducted in African and Mexican foci with different black fly populations, accounting for low applicability concerns. The O-150 PCR produced reliable results across different black fly species. It is possible that O-150 PCR has more accurate DTA characteristics than fly dissection, making the results of diagnostic studies using dissection as the gold-standard reference test unreliable. Furthermore, it is not feasible to perform both dissection and O-150 PCR on the same flies. Detailed results of the risk of bias and applicability assessments are shown in Table 6. One study also assessed the costs of O-150 PCR (PoolScreen) compared to fly dissection. The initial costs for O-150 PCR are significantly higher (~$45,000 for specialized equipment) than for dissection (~$2,000 for a dissection microscope). However, the long-term costs are much lower for O-150 PCR (~$3 per 100 black flies, including supplies and labor) compared to dissection (~$15 per 100 black flies). Cost comparisons may vary significantly between countries due to wage dependency. Tests for ocular morbidity (e.g., slit lamp examination) were also evaluated. The overarching clinical question addressed was: In populations at risk for onchocerciasis, which diagnostic tests or combinations of tests can validly and reliably demonstrate the interruption of Onchocerca volvulus transmission and predict the elimination of human onchocerciasis? In three endemic foci in Mali and Senegal, epidemiological evaluations were conducted using skin snip microscopy, and entomological evaluations were performed by examining black flies via O-150 PCR (PoolScreen, screening pools of 300 flies). In the Huehuetenango focus of Guatemala, Ov-16 serology, ophthalmological evaluations, and entomological evaluations using O-150 PCR were conducted. GRADE profile 1 summarizes the evidence for the clinical pathway, including the quality and certainty of evidence. The interruption of transmission (MDA stopped) and elimination of onchocerciasis were confirmed in some foci. However, the measurement of skin snip microfilariae prevalence was performed at the village level rather than the individual level. O-150 PCR of skin snips (index test) was compared with skin snip microscopy (reference test). Sensitivity ranged from 71% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 15% to 100%. Pooling of results was not possible due to heterogeneity and high risk of bias. Many studies used case-control systems or did not include participants without onchocerciasis, leading to unclear or high risk of bias. Skin snip microscopy is an imperfect reference standard, particularly in low-prevalence settings. Ov-16 serology (index test) was also compared with skin snip microscopy (reference test). Sensitivity ranged from 81% to 98%, and specificity ranged from 89% to 100%. Ov-16 serology measures exposure to O. volvulus and indirectly detects transmission. Pooling of results was not possible due to heterogeneity and high risk of bias. Many studies used case-control systems or did not include participants without onchocerciasis, leading to unclear or high risk of bias. Participants and serum samples were collected from various regions, which may be representative of broader populations. O-150 PCR (PoolScreen) in black flies (index test) was compared with dissection of black flies (reference test). No statistically significant differences in diagnostic accuracy were observed between the two methods. Newer DNA extraction methods with larger pool sizes performed similarly to traditional methods. Total costs depend on labor costs, which vary between countries. Dissection of flies is an imperfect reference standard, as it is not possible to perform both dissection and PoolScreen on the same flies.
